tip: The 'voi' command is simply the present 'voi' form: 'fare' gives 'fate', so 'fate silenzio' means (you all) be quiet.
Formal commands to someone you address as 'Lei' use the subjunctive: 'andare' gives 'vada' (go, formal).
'Gli' means to him, and here it attaches to the command: 'portate' + 'gli' = 'portategli'.
'Vorrei' is the conditional of 'volere' and is the polite way to order or ask: 'vorrei un caffè' means I'd like a coffee.
The 'loro' (they) future ends in '-anno': 'aumentare' gives 'aumenteranno' (they will increase).
'Prima di' takes the infinitive to mean before doing something: 'prima di uscire' means before going out.
A negative 'voi' command keeps the normal 'voi' form after 'non': 'non vi arrabbiate' means don't (you all) get angry.
Impersonal 'si' plus a verb means one or it, with no named subject: 'si scopre' means it gets found out.
'Ci' can mean into it or on it and attaches to the command: 'metti' + 'ci' = 'mettici', put more into it.
'Bere' has an irregular future built on the stem berr-: 'berrò' means I will drink, not the expected 'bevrò'.
'Stare per' plus the infinitive means to be about to do something: 'sta per iniziare' means it's about to start.
The future tense can express a guess about the present: 'costerà molto' means it probably costs a lot.
'Avresti' is the conditional of 'avere' and softens a request: 'avresti tempo' means would you have time.
Verbs in '-care' add an h in the future to keep the hard c sound: 'cercare' gives 'cercherò' (I will look for).
Verbs in '-giare' drop the i in the future: 'mangiare' gives 'mangerai' (you will eat), not 'mangierai'.
The passive uses 'essere' plus the past participle, which agrees with the subject: 'sarà servita' (feminine) means will be served.
'Dovremmo' is the conditional of 'dovere' and means should, for suggestions: 'dovremmo partire' means we should leave.
The future perfect, 'avrò' plus the participle, marks what finishes first: 'avrò risparmiato' means once I've saved.
The 'trapassato' (imperfect of 'avere' or 'essere' plus participle) marks an earlier past: 'avevamo camminato' means we had walked.
Conditional 'potere' is the polite could: 'potrebbe aiutarmi' means could you help me, the go-to softener with strangers.
'Farsi' means to do something for yourself: 'mi farei un bel bagno caldo' is I'd run myself a nice hot bath, a reflexive where English has none.
To forbid someone you call 'tu', Italian switches to the infinitive: 'parla' means speak, but 'non parlare' means don't speak.
The negative 'tu' command uses the infinitive with the pronoun glued on: 'non dirgli' means don't tell him.
'Mi piacerebbe' is literally it would please me: the thing liked is the subject, and the wanter is 'mi'.
'Quella' drops to quell' before a feminine word starting with a vowel: 'quell'offerta', not 'quella offerta'.
'Senza' adds 'di' before a pronoun: 'senza di noi', 'senza di me'. Before a noun it stands alone: 'senza zucchero'.
When talking about the future, Italian keeps the future after 'quando': 'quando avrò tempo' is literally when I will have time, where English uses the present.
The future can express a guess about the present: 'avrà trent'anni' = he must be about thirty.
Verbs like 'partire' form the future perfect with 'essere': 'sarò già partito' = I'll have already left, not with 'avere'.
After 'senza', Italian uses the infinitive, not the -ing form: 'senza dirci niente' = without telling us anything.
